words.intro: There is one situation where every German speaker chooses each word with care, and everyone is afraid of getting it wrong. It lasts about ten minutes, in a black coat, and then there is coffee and cake.

grammar[0].blocks[2].text: At a funeral, stay with whatever you always said. A sudden *du* will be noticed, and so will a sudden *Sie*.
grammar[0].fact: Germans wear black. Germany is strict about what happens afterwards: in most states even ashes must be buried in a cemetery.

grammar[1].blocks[1].text: The higher your German gets, the more you’ll be able to say. It’s good to know this. In the moments that count, three short words will do, and you’ll know which ones.
grammar[1].fact: C2 is what’s left: style, allusion, what’s not said. Most Germans don’t reach it in all registers. If you’ve come this far in a language that isn’t yours, you can read Thomas Mann and fill in a tax form, and very few natives enjoy both.

document.intro: A real set of rules from a war cemetery. It’s among the most careful German you’ll read: *Es wird gebeten*, *abzusehen*, *zu achten*. Nobody is told off, and nothing is left unsaid. Read rule 2 first.
document.fact: The Volksbund, whose name is on this notice, is a charity which looks after the graves of German war dead in many countries. It lives largely on donations. School groups still go out to help tend the graves, sometimes with young people from the other side.

reading.intro: Opa Heinz has died, at 91, in his chair, with the football on. It is a clear cold day in Essen. The whole Stammtisch has come in dark coats. Max has been asked to say a few words, and he has been working on them for four days, with this book. He has them on a card.
reading.photos[0].caption: Ein Friedhof in Essen, an einem gewöhnlichen Tag.
reading.fact: A German death notice in the paper, the *Traueranzeige*, is a form of its own, with a verse and the words *in stiller Trauer*, and the local paper has pages of them on a Saturday. Many older Germans read those first. After the funeral there’s the *Trauerkaffee*, or *Leichenschmaus*, and, as you’ve just seen, cake.
